extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_short: evidence for axioms in deductive sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate or explain the epistemic status of axioms, definitions, and demonstrations in deductive (demonstrative) sciences by examining their empirical origin, hypothetical character, and limits of certainty. Focuses on how inductive experience, habit, and assumptions underlie apparently necessary truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are inductions from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms (first principles) of demonstrative sciences rest on experimental evidence and are generalizations from experience, not truths known independently of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues the burden of proof lies on those who claim axioms are a priori; one should treat axioms as extensively supported inductions and demand argument for any other origin. Includes examples and historical discussion showing axioms were discovered gradually by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as practical generalizations (geometrical sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: What are commonly called definitions in deductive sciences are generalizations from experience that assert some properties and exclude others for convenience; the denial of accompanying properties is a fiction used to simplify reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat definitions as convenient suppositions to exclude modifying circumstances; recognize they are not exact descriptive truths but pragmatic abstractions used when modifiers are negligible or postponed for separate consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (demonstrative) sciences are also inductive and hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive sciences proceed by tracing consequences of assumptions; their conclusions are true only on those suppositions, making these sciences hypothetical as much as demonstrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating deductive arguments, separate (a) the demonstration (inference from assumptions) from (b) the empirical adequacy of the assumptions. The certainty of conclusions is conditional on how near the assumptions are to actual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty is limited to pure number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) applies only to propositions about pure number, distinct from quantity in the enlarged sense; outside pure number, hypotheses about units introduce potential error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing absolute, a priori certainty to geometry, mechanics, or arithmetic when applied to real-world quantities; check whether the propositions rest on the implicit assumption that all units/instances are equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra/arithmetic reasoning is not merely verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: Although algebraic and arithmetical manipulations use symbols and may seem like substitutions of language, at each step there is an induction/inference concerning things (numbers of things), not a mere change of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising symbolic proofs, insist on identifying the underlying generalizations about things (e.g., collections, numbers) that justify each symbolic transformation; do not accept 'purely verbal' accounts without accounting for their experiential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit/association makes experimental truths appear necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged intellectual habit of arranging phenomena according to a theory can cause those propositions, originally learned by experience, to seem self-evident or inconceivable in the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of claims that a truth is inconceivable or a priori merely because it is familiar; consider historical cases (laws of motion, chemical proportions) where familiarity produced the illusion of necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity should mean conditional certainty, not independence from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity in deductive sciences should be understood as 'necessarily following from certain axioms/definitions' (certainty of inference) rather than as evidence superior to experience; claims of necessity independent of observation require justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of 'necessary truth' by checking whether they rely on prior empirical establishment of the axioms/definitions; do not accept independence-from-experience as given without argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate evaluation of assumptions and inferential consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrative inquiry, one must treat the tracing of consequences from assumptions as distinct from ascertaining whether the assumptions themselves are true or sufficiently approximate truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, perform deductive work to get consequences ready, but always follow with observational or argumentative work to test how closely the assumptions match reality in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions may include existence claims (geometrical definition example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometrical 'definition' (e.g., of a circle) often implies not only the meaning of a term but also the existence of figures answering to that description—so definitions can function as first principles grounded in observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a 'definition' is used as a foundation, check whether it covertly asserts existence or empirical fact; treat such definitional assertions as inductive premises requiring evidential support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic propositions presuppose uniformity of units
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetical truths (like 1+1=2) implicitly assume that the units counted are of the same kind or equivalent (1=1 in the relevant respect); without that, numerical conclusions about other quantities become hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applied arithmetic/statistics, verify that units are comparable (weights, measures, currencies); recognize that converting number-equality to other-equalities introduces hypotheses that must be checked empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of deductive sciences equals certainty of inference, not of premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar certainty often ascribed to mathematical or deductive results is 'certainty of inference'—i.e., if the premises are true then conclusions follow—but this does not guarantee the premises' truth or exhaustive inclusion of relevant data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the reliability of deductive conclusions, differentiate logical validity from empirical soundness; ensure premises are scrutinized for completeness and approximation to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional hypothesis use in experiment design
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists often provisionally assume a theory or hypothesis (grouping known facts) to derive consequences and then devise experiments to test whether apparently conflicting phenomena can be reconciled with the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize hypothesis-as-tool: assumptions may be adopted to organize inquiry and must then be subjected to targeted experiments; an assumed hypothesis is not proof until experiments confirm consistency with observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental representation influences acceptance of theories
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientist's mental picture—formed by habit of representing phenomena according to certain laws—makes alternative arrangements feel unnatural and eventually inconceivable because they conflict with incorporated facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that cognitive familiarity can bias theory appraisal; actively attempt to represent phenomena under rival frameworks to avoid mistaking habit for logical impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and axioms can be treated as convenient fictions when modifiers are negligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The denial of accompanying properties in a 'definition' is a fiction used to exclude modifying circumstances when their influence is too trivial or when postponement is convenient for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simplified definitions/axioms pragmatically, but document which modifers are being excluded and later assess whether those exclusions materially affect results; avoid uncritical absolutizing of such fictions.
